title: Controlling Dark Squares | Sicilian, Accelerated Dragon | Top Theory Speedrun | GM Naroditsky
openingName: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Maroczy Bind

moves.spoken: The pawn on c4 hands the knight a potential outpost on d4 — but there is no rush to sit on it. The knight comes to c6 first; the d4-hole is a long-term weakness that will tell only once everything is developed.
moves.teaches: A hole is a permanent asset — occupy it when the rest of your pieces are ready, not on move one.
moves.plans: Develop first; the d4 outpost keeps.

moves.spoken: The fianchetto goes in. It concedes one thing — White can answer with the pawn to d4 and steer into a standard Maróczy Bind — but in return the g7-bishop gets a magnificent long diagonal.
moves.teaches: Every setup has a trade-off; here g6 allows a transposition but earns the Dragon's best piece.
moves.plans: Fianchetto and fight for the dark squares.

moves.spoken: With the bishop on g7 Black is already comfortably better: the dark squares in the centre are dominated, and White's light-squared bishop is stuck behind its own c4-, d3- and e4-pawns — a big pawn, not a piece.
moves.teaches: A bishop hemmed in by its own fixed pawns is dead weight; play against it.
moves.plans: Trade the good pieces, leave White the bad bishop.

moves.spoken: The pawn to d6 improves the position and, more to the point, prepares to trade off the f3-knight with the bishop to g4 — the knight is White's main guard of the d4 square. The g8-knight can wait.
moves.teaches: Target the piece defending your key square; here the f3-knight guards d4.
moves.plans: Play Bg4 to remove the d4 defender.

moves.spoken: The bishop steps to g4, clamping down on d4 by threatening to trade the very piece that controls it. This is classic positional chess — remove the defender of the square you want.
moves.teaches: To win a square, trade off its defender.
moves.plans: Exchange on f3, then dominate d4.

moves.spoken: Eliminate the knight while the chance is there. Trading the light-squared bishops is only fine for Black, but removing White's f3-knight — the guard of d4 — is the real prize, so take it now before it can slip away.
moves.teaches: Prefer the trade that removes the opponent's most useful piece, even at the cost of your own good one.

moves.spoken: The Botvinnik setup: fianchetto plus the pawn to e6, carving out e7 as the developing square for the g8-knight. The pawns stand like teeth, gripping the central light squares White can never occupy.
moves.teaches: The Botvinnik pawn structure (pawns on e6/d6/c5 with a fianchetto) clamps the central light squares.
moves.plans: Route the knight via e7 and keep the clamp.

moves.spoken: The knight develops to e7 and the whole army stands in harmony — every piece has a clear role, all bearing down on the centre. The plan is simply to keep squeezing the central squares.
moves.teaches: Harmony first: when every piece has a defined job, the plan plays itself.
moves.plans: Castle, then expand where you're stronger.

moves.spoken: The pawn to h6 does two jobs: it provokes the capture on e7 — White handing over the dark-squared bishop for the inferior e7-knight, exactly the trade Black wants — and it clears the way to castle without fearing a bishop battery on h6.
moves.teaches: Provoke the exchange of the opponent's good bishop for your least valuable piece.
moves.plans: Take back on e7 with the queen, keeping the knight for d4.

moves.spoken: Castling completes development and marks the exit from the opening. Black is clearly better — call it around minus one and a half — with the dark squares, the better structure, and a clear plan; now those pluses must become something concrete.
moves.teaches: A positional edge is potential energy — the work is converting it into a concrete threat.
moves.plans: Expand on the queenside and open a file.

moves.spoken: The unassuming pawn to a6 is the first step of the real plan: preparing the b5 break to prise open the queenside where Black is stronger.
moves.teaches: Big breaks are prepared quietly — a6 lays the ground for b5.
moves.plans: Follow with b5 and open lines against White's king.

moves.spoken: Now — and only now — the knight lands on d4, chosen at the most opportune moment rather than the first. It cements the grip while the queenside break is readied.
moves.teaches: Occupy your outpost when it does the most work, not the instant it's available.
moves.plans: Combine the d4 knight with the b5 break.

moves.spoken: The break lands: the pawn to b5 strikes the queenside open, and White is already close to lost — the pieces are too loose to meet it.
moves.teaches: A well-prepared pawn break against an uncoordinated position is decisive.
moves.plans: Open the b- and a-files and hunt the pieces.

moves.spoken: After the pawns come off, the queen on a4 is simply trapped — the b5 break has cut off its squares. When a familiar plan meets careless play, it works like a charm.
moves.teaches: An advanced queen with no retreat is a target; a pawn break can wall it in.
moves.plans: Win the queen, keep every other plus.

moves.spoken: The knight to f3 with check is the clean finish — a fork that ends it at once, far quicker than grinding a simplified endgame a queen up.
moves.teaches: Up material, still take the forcing fork when it ends the game outright.

moves.spoken: The opening verdict on the c4 Maróczy: the fianchetto is not technically the most precise, since the pawn to d4 lets White steer into the standard Maróczy Bind where theory prefers White. But Black's plan here — the Botvinnik clamp and the b5 break — is easy to play and very strong in practice.
moves.teaches: Objective best and practically best can differ; a clear, easy plan is worth a shade of theory.
